To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
microRNAs are regulated in a light-dependent manner in the retina and that neuronal cells have a high turnover of microRNIs.
the levels of several microRNAs are regulated by different levels of light in the retina, with transcriptional and decay regulation being involved.
microRNA concentrations in the retina are rapidly regulated by light and are linked to the neuronal function of photoreceptors.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of the microRNA expression in the mammalian retina and the turnover of microRNas in neurons.
the characterization of light-regulated retinal microRNAs.
the characterization of microRNA regulation in retinal neurons and the identification of a common feature of microRNA metabolism in neuronal cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the miR-182 cluster, miRNA-204, and the miR-211 family are light-responsive in the mouse retina, and that microRNA metabolism is accelerated in neuronal cells and is regulated by neuronal activity.
the miR-204/211/183 cluster is light regulated and that the light-dependent regulation of miR-204 and miR-183 is mediated by a rapid decay of mature miR-204.
light adaptation of the retina is mediated by the rapid regulation of neuronal microRNAs.

microRNAs are rapidly degraded and their levels are regulated by transcription and/or translation in retinal neurons.
microRNAs are regulated by light in the retina.
the retina is an ideal model for studying the role of microRNAs and other posttranscriptional mechanisms in the adaptation to light and dark.

neuronal microRNAs have high turnover rates and that their expression is linked to neuronal activity, suggesting that microRNAs may be involved in synaptic plasticity.
